gongwen.1.tier_reason: Core: every drafting task starts here; it stops the most common cause of rework.
gongwen.1.why: The biggest source of rework in official documents is not the writing but the wrong recipient or a missed deadline. Asking first stops the error before drafting begins. With few, precise questions, the user doesn't feel interrogated.
gongwen.1.example:
> *Demonstration:* User: “Write me a notice.”
>
> Reply: “Sure. Three things first: 1. Is it a meeting notice or a work arrangement? 2. It goes out in the name of the ×× Department of ×× Province; which units is it addressed to? 3. What is the core matter, and what are the deadlines?”
gongwen.1.breakdown:
- Only three questions, covering document type, reporting relationship, and matter and deadline.
- “In the name of the ×× Department of ×× Province”: the issuer follows the user's unit; nothing is assumed.
- Questions come with options, making them cheaper to answer.
gongwen.1.overdo:
> Please provide: issuing body, primary recipient, copy recipients, classification, classification period, urgency, signatory, date of issue, number of copies, attachments…

The fault: a dozen fields at once, like filling in a form. The user will give up.
gongwen.1.when_not:
- Pure polishing or proofreading, where the draft already contains every element.
- When the user's message has already made all the key information clear.
gongwen.1.exercise: The user says, “Write a request asking for money.” Write the three questions you would ask.
gongwen.1.check: Three questions or fewer? Once answered, can you fix the issuer, the recipient and the core matter?
gongwen.1.adjacent:
- gongwen.2: choosing the document type; what clarification yields often decides the type directly.
- gongwen.3: inventorying the material; clarification asks for elements, the inventory reads the material.

gongwen.2.tier_reason: Common: needed whenever the user hasn't named the type, or has named the wrong one.
gongwen.2.why: A wrong document type is a hard error no matter how well the rest is written: write a request as a report and the superior won't reply to it. Giving the reason lets the user know why, and leaves the final decision with them, without overstepping.
gongwen.2.example: > *Demonstration:* “You are asking your superior for funding and need an answer, so I suggest a request (qingshi) rather than a report (baogao): a report doesn't require a reply, while a request must be approved. The final choice is yours.”
gongwen.2.breakdown:
- The basis is whether the superior must reply, which is a matter of reporting relationship.
- One sentence contrasts two easily confused types.
- “The final choice is yours”: advice, not a decision made for them.
gongwen.2.overdo:
> Based on your needs, the document type should be a “request-report”.

The fault: “request-report” is a common misuse that merges two types, exactly the error this step exists to stop.
gongwen.2.when_not: - When the user has clearly specified a type and it isn't a misuse; no need to argue it again.
gongwen.2.exercise: The ×× Department of ×× Province needs to inform a peer unit of a work arrangement and ask for its cooperation. Choose the type and give one sentence of reasoning.
gongwen.2.check: Does the reason rest on the reporting relationship (upward, downward, lateral) and on whether a reply is needed?
gongwen.2.adjacent:
- gongwen.4: tone by situation; once the type is set, the tone follows.
- gongwen.6: standard structure; the type determines the closing formula.

gongwen.3.tier_reason: Core: official documents must rest on evidence, and this is where the evidence comes from.
gongwen.3.why: Official documents need a basis for everything. Reading the material in full means you don't guess its contents from file names. The summary turns scattered material into a usable list: every sentence in the draft can be matched to a source, and gaps show at a glance. If a figure is missing, ask the user rather than filling it in yourself.
gongwen.3.example:
> *Demonstration:* Material summary:
> Core fact: the ×× Department of ×× Province plans to hold professional training next month (source: work plan provided by the user).
> Policy basis: not provided by the user; to be supplied.
> Usable wording: “further improve professional competence” (source: paragraph 2 of the user's material).
> Gaps: number of trainees and source of funding; confirm with the user.
gongwen.3.breakdown:
- Every item has a source, answering “where is this from?”
- The policy basis is marked “to be supplied”, not made up.
- Gaps are listed separately and turned into questions for the user.
gongwen.3.overdo:
> In line with the spirit of relevant policies and the requirements of higher-level arrangements, and in light of our department's actual situation, this work has achieved remarkable results in recent years.

The fault: “relevant policies” and “remarkable results” have no source at all; it is stock filler from nowhere.
gongwen.3.when_not: - Pure polishing tasks only need a full read of the draft, not research.
gongwen.3.exercise: Take a work document at hand and write a four-line material summary, each line with its source, plus one gap.
gongwen.3.check: Can every fact and figure in the draft be traced to a source in the summary?
gongwen.3.adjacent:
- gongwen.1: clarifying requirements, which asks for the elements.
- gongwen.7: reading it back; check the summary again when verifying content.

gongwen.4.tier_reason: Core: every document has a direction, and the tone has to match it.
gongwen.4.why: For the same matter, “please” to a superior, “must” to a subordinate and “we would ask” to a peer tell readers at once what the relationship is and what is expected. Mismatched tone makes superiors feel ordered about and leaves subordinates unsure whether to act.
gongwen.4.example:
> *Demonstration:* Upward: “We submit the above for your approval.”
>
> Downward: “All units are to submit by the stated deadline.”
>
> Lateral: “We would ask for your unit's support, and look forward to your reply.”
gongwen.4.breakdown:
- Upward uses “for your approval”: the decision is handed to the superior.
- Downward uses “are to submit”: the action and deadline are clear.
- Lateral uses “we would ask” and “look forward to your reply”: a consultative voice.
gongwen.4.overdo:
> (To a superior) Your unit must reply within three days; failing that, approval will be assumed.

The fault: an upward document in a downward, commanding tone, even setting a deadline for the superior. A serious breach of courtesy.
gongwen.4.when_not: - There is no occasion to skip this, only a question of which register. Internal notices may be a little looser, but never colloquial.
gongwen.4.exercise: Write the same sentence, “Please provide the ×× materials”, three ways: upward, downward and lateral.
gongwen.4.check: Do the closing formula and the key verbs match the direction of the document?
gongwen.4.adjacent:
- gongwen.2: choosing the document type.
- gongwen.5: length control, also a matter of fitting the situation.

gongwen.5.tier_reason: Common: a judgment made on every draft, though usually a quick one.
gongwen.5.why: Readers of an urgent notice want what to do and when; each extra paragraph of background is a delay. Readers of a major matter want the basis and the considerations; too short looks careless. Length itself conveys the weight of the matter.
gongwen.5.example:
> *Demonstration:* Urgent: “A special meeting will be held tomorrow morning. Heads of all divisions are asked to attend on time. Venue: Department Meeting Room ××.”
>
> Major: set out in three parts, “Background and Basis”, “Main Content” and “Safeguards”, each developed in turn.
gongwen.5.breakdown:
- The urgent version has only time, matter and audience, no background.
- The major version carries its length through a structure of levels, not piled-up description.
gongwen.5.overdo:
> (Urgent meeting notice) In order to thoroughly implement… further raise awareness, unify thinking and strengthen responsibility… after study, it has been decided to hold a meeting tomorrow.

The fault: an urgent matter stuffed with stock preamble, the key information pushed to the end.
gongwen.5.when_not: - When the user has a clear length requirement, follow the user.
gongwen.5.exercise: Cut a 300-character meeting notice to under 80 characters while keeping every element.
gongwen.5.check: Within the first paragraph, can the reader get what is to be done, who does it, and when?
gongwen.5.adjacent:
- gongwen.4: tone by situation.
- gongwen.7: reading it back, which cuts the wordy parts.

gongwen.6.tier_reason: Common: applied to every document, mostly by following the standard template.
gongwen.6.why: Format is the lifeblood of an official document: readers rely on a fixed structure to find information fast, and any missing or misplaced element is a hard error. Better plain content than a slip in format.
gongwen.6.example:
> *Demonstration:*
> Notice of the ×× Department of ×× Province on Holding Professional Training
> All divisions:
> 一、Training dates
> （一）……
> 1.……
> (end of body)
> ×× Department of ×× Province
> (date of writing)
gongwen.6.breakdown:
- Title: issuing body + “on” + subject + document type.
- The recipient line starts flush left, with standard forms of address.
- Level numbering: 一、（一）1.（1）, with no skipped levels; with fewer levels, use only 一、 and （一）, or 一、 and 1.
- The signature matches the issuing body; the date of writing uses Arabic numerals, with no padding zeros in month or day.
- Upward documents (requests, reports) must also name the signatory, and a request gives a contact person and phone number in the note.
gongwen.6.overdo:
> Notice About Training!!
> Hi everyone:
> 1、Time…
> 一、Place…

The fault: the title lacks the issuing body and uses exclamation marks, the recipient line is colloquial, and the numbering is mixed up and inverted.
gongwen.6.when_not: - There is no occasion to skip it; the template is only a structural reference, not something to copy mechanically.
gongwen.6.exercise: Take a meeting arrangement that has only a body and add the title, recipient and signature.
gongwen.6.check: Are all five elements present? Is numbering used in the order 一、（一）1.（1）, without skipping or mixing levels?
gongwen.6.adjacent:
- gongwen.2: choosing the document type, which decides the end of the title and the closing formula.
- gongwen.7: reading it back.

gongwen.7.why: Eyes skip over errors; the mouth doesn't. Where you stumble reading silently, readers will stumble too. The common-errors list then catches the frequent hard errors one by one: wrong document type, wrong closing formula, several matters in one document.
gongwen.7.example:
> *Demonstration:* Original: “为了进一步更好地加强做好该项工作的开展。”
> *Gloss:* “In order to further better strengthen and do well the carrying-out of this work.”
>
> After reading it back: “为做好该项工作。”
> *Gloss:* “To do this work well.”
gongwen.7.breakdown:
- “Further better strengthen and do well”: you stumble the moment you read it; one layer stacked on another.
- “The carrying-out of this work”: verb and object repeat; cut it.
- The meaning is unchanged and the length is halved.
gongwen.7.overdo:
> After a comprehensive self-check, this document has no problems whatsoever; the format is fully standard and the language highly concise.

The fault: it claims a check but can't show a single change. The check is a formality.
gongwen.7.when_not: - This step can't be skipped, only shortened: even a pure polishing task needs one silent read-through.
gongwen.7.exercise: Take a piece you wrote, read it through silently once, and cut at least three redundant words or phrases.
gongwen.7.check: Can you list at least one specific change made after reading it back? If not, you didn't read it.
gongwen.7.adjacent:
- gongwen.6: standard structure.
- gongwen.8: a word on delivery, which comes only after the check.

gongwen.8.tier_reason: Common: one sentence at handover on nearly every task.
gongwen.8.why: The user may not see what choices you made in the draft. One sentence tells them what can be adjusted and where the emphasis lies if a superior asks, and keeps the final decision with them.
gongwen.8.example: > *Demonstration:* “This version is fairly formal, suited to going out in the name of the ×× Department of ×× Province. If it is only for circulation within the department, the opening background paragraph can go. Shall I adjust it?”
gongwen.8.breakdown:
- “Fairly formal”: states the current choice.
- “If… can…”: offers one specific direction for adjustment.
- It ends on a question, handing the decision back to the user.
gongwen.8.overdo:
> Above is the document carefully crafted for you. I hope it helps, and feel free to reach out with any questions!

The fault: pleasantries with no word on the choices made, which amounts to saying nothing.
gongwen.8.when_not: - When the user explicitly wants only the finished draft and no explanation, cut it to one sentence.
gongwen.8.exercise: Write a one-sentence delivery note for a downward notice, with the current tone and one adjustable direction.
gongwen.8.check: Does the note contain one specific adjustable item?
gongwen.8.adjacent: - gongwen.9: style memory; the user's response to this note is what gets recorded.

gongwen.9.tier_reason: Common: the engine's distinctive feature, used once the user has given feedback and consent.
gongwen.9.why: If the user once said “too wordy”, the next draft should be shorter. Recording preferences makes the drafts fit better over time. Asking consent and never recording classified matters are what make it trustworthy. It is a design feature of this engine that depends on a persistent profile, not a general writing technique.
gongwen.9.example:
> *Demonstration:* Profile entry: “Preference: notice bodies kept to one page. Source: user feedback, ‘too long’.”
>
> Before writing it: “I've noticed you prefer shorter notices. Shall I note that in your style profile so I write them that way next time?”
gongwen.9.breakdown:
- The entry records the preference and its source, not the specific content.
- It asks before writing, and gets consent.
- Nothing classified is recorded.
gongwen.9.overdo:
> Automatically recorded: the personnel list, funding amounts and internal discussion from this notice.

The fault: no consent, and it records sensitive and possibly classified content.
gongwen.9.when_not:
- When the user hasn't agreed.
- When the content involves personnel, funds or classified matters; record only preferences, never facts.
gongwen.9.exercise: From one line of user feedback, “make the tone a bit firmer”, write a profile entry and a sentence asking consent.
gongwen.9.check: Does the entry contain only a preference and no specific matters? Has consent been given?
gongwen.9.adjacent:
- gongwen.8: a word on delivery.
- gongwen.1: clarifying requirements; read the profile before clarifying next time.
